name: Nipple-to-nipple ratio

card.summary: A chest-width proportion some physique-focused people measure to judge how wide or narrow the chest looks, used to guide training emphasis and posing.
card.note: A community measurement idea; no standard ideal range appears in published research.

quick.overview:
The nipple-to-nipple ratio compares the distance between the nipples with another body dimension, such as chest or shoulder width, as a rough read on chest proportions. In forums it is discussed alongside shoulder-to-waist ratio and other proportion measurements.

The payoff is a way to describe how the chest reads visually, and to decide whether to emphasise pec and shoulder development. Published research on the metric as an aesthetic measure was not located; related chest-width ratios appear in clinical imaging, a different context.
quick.how: People measure it themselves with a tape or photos, then compare it with figures shared in forums. Training log communities more commonly use shoulder, waist and chest circumference targets based on golden-ratio style proportions.
quick.risks: Low physical risk. Measurements vary with posture, flexing and breathing, and nipple position differs naturally between people, so numbers circulating online are informal.

lead: The nipple-to-nipple ratio is a proportion some people in looksmaxxing and physique communities use to describe chest width, comparing nipple spacing with a reference width such as the chest or rib cage. One looksmax.org thread asks about the ideal range, with the poster saying their own seems too wide and planning to measure it themselves.[1]

Bodybuilding communities more often discuss proportion through shoulder-to-waist and golden-ratio targets. A T Nation training log, for instance, calculates goal measurements for shoulders, arms, chest, thighs and calves from golden-ratio style calculations.[2]

Medical literature uses chest-width ratios in other settings, such as mediastinal-width to chest-width on X-rays in trauma and chest configuration studies in children with kidney disease.[3][4] These are not aesthetic standards.

chain: Measure nipple spacing against chest width
Judge how wide or narrow the chest reads
Choose training emphasis (pecs, shoulders) or posing
angle.text: People use it as a descriptive proportion for how the chest looks, then adjust training or posing to change the overall visual balance. Nipple placement itself is anatomical and is not changed by training.

paras: Community discussion treats nipple placement as part of chest aesthetics, with phrases like 'nipple insertions' used for how nipples sit on the chest.[1] No agreed formula or ideal range for a nipple-to-nipple ratio appears in the forum thread, and the poster in the main discussion asked for one.[1]

Training communities set target ratios between shoulders, waist and limbs, sometimes from golden-ratio calculations.[2] Competitors also talk about shoulder-to-waist ratios as a width illusion, with one coach-style reply noting a front lat spread creates the appearance of width.[5]

No studies found. Related but different research: radiology studies use a mediastinal-to-chest-width ratio to assess possible aortic injury after blunt trauma, and one found it not sufficiently sensitive or specific to be clinically useful.[3] A 2023 paediatric study measured thoracic dimensions in children with cystinosis and other kidney disease.[4]

lore.intro: The metric appears sporadically in looksmaxxing and physique forums as one of many proportion ideas.[1][2]

claims.claim: There is an ideal nipple-to-nipple ratio that determines how wide the chest looks
claims.believers: Forum users ask what range is ideal and measure their own to see whether it is 'too wide'.[1]
claims.experts: No published study defines an aesthetic ideal for nipple spacing; chest-width ratios in the literature serve clinical imaging.[3][4]

claims.claim: Proportion targets such as golden-ratio measurements guide physique development
claims.believers: Lifters calculate goal shoulder, chest and limb measurements from ideal ratios and train toward them.[2]
claims.experts: No published study tests these targets for attractiveness.
